items.dek: All instances occur on public roads and curbs, an unstructured setting, so the cap is E3 throughout. Waymo's commercial driverless service (≈3,500 vehicles, ~500k paid rides/week, 220M+ rider-only miles, freeway and airport curbside service, 24/7 availability), corroborated by Zoox in Las Vegas, supports E3 for instances 0 (urban core, 30), 1 (suburban, 20), 2 (airport/freeway, 15) and 3 (late night, 15) = 80 weight. items.notes: Already H.264 High/yuv420p + AAC-LC and under 45 MB, so it was stream-copied rather than re-encoded (a re-encode could only lose quality). WHAT IT IS: a scripted, pre-rendered text-to-speech showcase (a fan-made 'spec ad'), NOT a real-time conversation, NOT a cloning demo and NOT an official product launch. Author's own bio says 'ex-ElevenLabs'; his self-reply says: 'This is a personal spec project. Not affiliated with or commissioned by ElevenLabs. Just a fan of what v4 can do, showing off something I've been waiting a long time for.' Voice = Eleven v4 per the author (post does not say whether standard v4 or v4 Turbo, nor which preset/cloned voice, nor which tags/prompts were used). Visuals appear to be AI-generated video (post labelled 'Made with AI'); the video model/tool is NOT named anywhere we could find. HOW NATURAL IT SOUNDS: I cannot listen to audio. What can be said from analysis: (1) speech-to-text recognised every scripted line cleanly, including the shouted line, the whispered lines and the Italian-accented word; (2) it contains non-verbal vocalisations (opening laugh, scream, a collapse/sob-like 'fall apart' line, a sung line) - the exact behaviours the script says AI voices 'can't do'; (3) delivery dynamic range is wide: RMS -18.2 dBFS (scream, peak -3.4) vs -28.8/-30.0 dBFS (whispers). Subjective realism is the author's claim ('INSANE') plus ~1.9M views; there is no blind test of this clip. For the talk: play it live with sound, then let the audience judge.

datasets.notes: Text: a fully robot-exposed occupation had wages 7.1% lower (95% CI 5.4% to 8.9%) and lost 34.2% of its jobs (95% CI 16.4% to 52.0%) over about 20 years relative to an unexposed occupation in the same industry. datasets.title: Robot adoption scenarios: year robots become cost-competitive
datasets.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" main text (2085 / 2050) and Appendix E / Appendix Figure 12 (janitors 2095; rapid: "2050s")
datasets.notes: Other stated timeline points: business as usual - robots cost-competitive for 10% of human work "until the 2060s"; ~40 years at 3%/yr; by 2075 robots can do 90% of physical tasks in the "broadening" variant. Rapid advances (12%/yr hardware, 6%/yr other costs) - 10% of work time by "around 2040", robot janitors in the 2050s; automating 90% of today's physical work still takes 53 years. By 2040 business-as-usual projects robots cost-competitive for 2.5 million jobs in occupations where robots can do at least 85% of tasks (600,000 to 3 million across the 95% and 75% thresholds) - the authors call 2.5 million "more of a ceiling on job loss than a central estimate"; the China trade shock cost an estimated 2-2.4 million jobs over 1999-2011.

arXiv received a record 40,363 submissions in September 2026 — double September 2024 (20,569) and 4x September 2016 (9,869).

ICLR 2026: 19,525 submissions, 76,139 reviews — submissions up ~6x since 2022 (3,391).
NeurIPS 2026 received 30,709 main-track submissions — triple 2022 (10,411).
NeurIPS 2026 desk-rejected 18.4% of position-paper submissions (178 of 969) as AI-generated.
75% of all new code at Google is now AI-generated, up from 50% last fall and 25% in 2024.
